one_liner: SIMD-accelerated C CSV parser/writer (AVX-512/AVX2) beating csvkit and PapaParse; monorepo now deprecated.
what_it_does: C library for parsing and writing CSV, exposing a callback-based streaming parser, a fgetcsv-style row iterator with early exit, a fast row-count-only mode, and field transforms (case, trim, hash, base64). Ships bindings for Node.js, Python, and PHP on top of the same core. Not a drop-in for csvkit's Python CLI or API; it is a separate C API and CLI with its own flag syntax.
how_it_is_fast: Vectorized byte scanning for delimiters/quotes/newlines using AVX-512 mask compares (or AVX2/SSE2 movemask + ctz, ARM NEON fallback) instead of a byte-at-a-time state machine. Input files are zero-copy memory-mapped with kernel read-ahead hints and read through an L3-sized ring buffer. A chunk-splitting API (mmap + split-at-row-boundaries) enables multi-threaded parallel parsing, described in the header as a '1 Billion Row Challenge technique'.
when_to_use: Row-counting or bulk parsing of large CSVs on x86-64 with AVX-512 or AVX2 available
Embedding a small C parser/writer directly into a C/C++ codebase rather than shelling out to a Python tool
Node.js/Python/PHP apps that need faster synchronous CSV parsing than PapaParse/csv-parse for one-shot batch jobs
Workloads needing early-exit row iteration (stop after N matching rows) without loading the whole file
Multi-core boxes where parallel chunked parsing of one large file is worth the added complexity
when_not_to_use: Production systems: the whole monorepo is archived/deprecated by its own author, moved to separate cisv-core/cisv-cli/bindings repos with unclear activity
CPUs without AVX2/AVX-512 (older x86, some cloud instance types) — falls back to SSE2/NEON/scalar with speed not benchmarked
Anywhere `miller` is an option: the author's own table shows miller ~14x faster than cisv on the same 1M-row count
Windows — unsupported (README lists it as 'planned... maybe')
Teams needing a mature, community-supported CSV toolkit rather than a single-author experimental project (91 stars, author calls it 'still evolving')

integration.form: source-drop / static lib (CMake or Makefile build) plus separate Node.js/Python/PHP native bindings
integration.dependencies: none for core C library; Node.js 14+, Python 3.7+, or PHP 7.4+ toolchains for the respective bindings
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX-512 or AVX2 preferred, SSE2 fallback), ARM64/NEON; Linux and macOS only, no Windows
integration.thread_safety: not documented globally; parallel API requires one parser instance per thread, each parsing its own chunk
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — different C API/CLI flags than csvkit's Python interface, not a compatible replacement

gotchas: Repo is marked DEPRECATED in its own README; code has moved to split repos (cisv-core, cisv-cli, cisv-nodejs, cisv-python, cisv-php)
Peak throughput requires AVX-512; on AVX2/SSE2/NEON hardware speed is unverified
Author states the code changed during writing of the benchmark blog post, so published numbers may not match current source
Row iterator's returned field pointers are only valid until the next call — no copy-out API mentioned for retention
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick cisv only for a minimal, vendorable C library/CLI using raw SIMD intrinsics with no dependencies; zsv (same category) does the same mmap+SIMD row-counting approach but is faster in its own benchmarks, more actively maintained, and has broader language coverage, so prefer zsv unless you specifically want cisv's smaller C surface.
verified_claims_summary: Author's blog, built with -O3 -march=native -mavx512f -mavx512bw on an unspecified Intel Core i9, reports CLI row-counting of a 1M-row/98MB CSV: miller 0.004s, cisv 0.055s, wc -l 0.083s, rust-csv 0.664s, csvkit 9.788s (~178x over csvkit, but ~14x slower than miller in the same table). Separately, Node.js synchronous parsing measured cisv at 60.80 MB/s vs PapaParse 25.12 MB/s (~2.4x) and csv-parse 14.67 MB/s.
status_note: Abandoned/archived, and the monorepo itself declares itself deprecated in favor of split successor repos; MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but pick a maintained fork or successor repo before depending on it.
